feedback: Target (full command) looks like: there was inherited variation (pale and dark moths); dark colour was an adaptation suiting the sooty trees; birds ate the more visible pale moths (a selection pressure), so more dark moths survived and passed on their colour through reproduction (natural selection); over many generations the population became mostly dark (evolution). The pale form becoming rare is not extinction, because pale and dark moths are the same species. A species is extinct when none are left anywhere (e.g. the dodo), and endangered when it still survives but is at high risk of dying out (e.g. the tiger).

Partial command: several terms used correctly but not in a coherent sequence, or adaptation blurred with natural selection, or evolution with natural selection — ask the learner to re-order and re-tell.
Gap: terms used as loose labels, out of order, or extinct confused with endangered — return to the gallery contrast pair and the ordered chain before retelling.

A single organism can possess adaptations (features), but it does not EVOLVE within its lifetime, and it does not adapt in the heritable, across-generations sense — evolution and the process of adaptation apply to the population over generations; redirect if the learner attaches an individual's lifetime change to these process words.
activities.intendedInsight: Genuine command shows in sequenced USE within a live narrative — using each term precisely and in order, and cleanly distinguishing extinct from endangered with examples — not in reciting isolated definitions.
learnerActions: Tell the story of how a population of moths in a sooty, polluted city came to be mostly dark-coloured, using these words in a sensible order as you go: variation, adaptation, natural selection, reproduction.

Explain why 'extinct' would NOT be the right word if pale moths became very rare in the city: pale and dark moths are colour forms of the same species, and extinction means a whole species (every member, everywhere) has died out. Then say how 'extinct' differs from 'endangered', using real species as examples.

Answer probing follow-ups in your own words: what exactly was the selection pressure in the moth story? Could a single moth 'evolve' in its lifetime, or does that word apply to the population over generations — and which word goes with which? Give a real animal that is extinct and one that is endangered, saying why each word fits. Where does 'mutation' fit as a source of new variation?
activities.title: Tell the moth story using the words in sequence (use-in-context)
